quick: Take with or immediately after food
No demonstrated risk in studies; monitor neonate
Present in milk; monitor infant for bradycardia
summary: Metoprolol tartrate is an immediate-release beta-1 selective (cardioselective) adrenergic blocker for hypertension, angina pectoris, and to reduce cardiovascular mortality after acute myocardial infarction in hemodynamically stable patients. It slows heart rate, reduces AV conduction, and lowers blood pressure. It is taken with or after meals and must never be stopped abruptly; taper over 1-2 weeks to avoid rebound ischemia.
indications: Hypertension (to lower blood pressure and reduce cardiovascular risk)
Acute myocardial infarction — to reduce cardiovascular mortality in hemodynamically stable patients (with IV metoprolol therapy)

dosage.n: Titrate at weekly (or longer) intervals; max effect of a dose ~1 week
Increase at weekly intervals to response or pronounced HR slowing

dosage.d: 50 mg every 6 h for 48 h, then 100 mg twice daily
dosage.n: Start after tolerated IV metoprolol; for intolerant patients start 25-50 mg q6h

dosage.d: Initiate at low doses and titrate gradually

admin: Take regularly and continuously, preferably with or immediately following meals
Take at approximately the same time each day
Do not interrupt or discontinue without physician advice
When discontinuing, taper gradually over 1-2 weeks
Measure blood pressure near the end of the dosing interval to confirm 24-hour control
moa: Metoprolol is a beta-1 selective (cardioselective) adrenergic receptor blocker; this preference is not absolute and at higher plasma concentrations it also inhibits beta-2 receptors in bronchial and vascular muscle. It has no intrinsic sympathomimetic activity. It slows the sinus rate and decreases AV nodal conduction. Antihypertensive effects are attributed to reduced cardiac output, decreased central sympathetic outflow, and suppression of renin; antianginal effect is from reduced myocardial oxygen demand.

absolute: Systolic blood pressure <100 mmHg (in MI setting)
Sick sinus syndrome without a pacemaker
relative: Peripheral vascular disease (may aggravate arterial insufficiency)
Thyrotoxicosis (abrupt withdrawal may precipitate thyroid storm)
monitor: Heart rate and blood pressure during titration
Hypoglycemia signs in fasting or vomiting patients
Anaphylaxis (may be unresponsive to usual epinephrine doses)

preg: Published observational studies have not demonstrated an association of adverse developmental outcomes with maternal metoprolol use. Metoprolol crosses the placenta; neonates may be at risk of hypotension, hypoglycemia, bradycardia and respiratory depression and should be observed. Untreated hypertension and MI in pregnancy carry maternal and fetal risk.
lact: Metoprolol is present in human milk. Monitor the breastfed infant for bradycardia and other signs of beta-blockade.
renal: Systemic availability and half-life in renal failure do not differ to a clinically significant degree from normal subjects; no dosage reduction needed. Hemodialysis is unlikely to remove it appreciably.
hepatic: Eliminated mainly by hepatic biotransformation (primarily CYP2D6). In hepatic impairment, initiate at low doses and titrate gradually while monitoring closely.

major: Strong CYP2D6 inhibitors (quinidine, fluoxetine, paroxetine, propafenone) — double metoprolol concentrations and reduce cardioselectivity
Catecholamine-depleting drugs (reserpine, MAO inhibitors) — additive hypotension/bradycardia
Clonidine — beta-blockers may exacerbate rebound hypertension on clonidine withdrawal
moderate: Digitalis glycosides, diltiazem, verapamil — slow AV conduction; increased bradycardia risk
Other antihypertensives — additive blood pressure lowering
minor: Other (moderate/weak) CYP2D6 inhibitors likely to increase metoprolol concentration
interactions.food: Take with or immediately after meals for consistency.
interactions.alcohol: Avoid; alcohol may potentiate hypotension and dizziness.
interactions.diagnostics: May mask tachycardia from hypoglycemia or hyperthyroidism.

serious: Severe bradycardia or worsening AV block
rare: Worsening angina or MI on abrupt withdrawal
emergency: Anaphylaxis unresponsive to usual epinephrine doses

monitoring: Blood pressure (near end of dosing interval)
Blood glucose in diabetic, fasting, or vomiting patients
Clinical status during titration and on discontinuation
counsel: Take regularly and continuously, preferably with or immediately after meals
Do not interrupt or stop therapy without consulting your physician
If a dose is missed, take only the next scheduled dose; do not double up
Avoid driving or operating machinery until your response is known
Contact your physician if you have difficulty breathing
Inform any physician or dentist that you take this medication before surgery
Be aware of hypoglycemia risk if fasting or vomiting
pk: 3 to 4 hours (7-9 hours in CYP2D6 poor metabolizers)
Lower doses (100 mg) may not maintain full 24-hour effect
20-25C (68-77F); excursions 15-30C; protect from moisture and heat, light-resistant container
pearls: Never discontinue abruptly; taper over 1-2 weeks to avoid rebound angina/MI, especially in ischemic heart disease
Immediate-release tartrate: lower doses may need divided/more frequent dosing for 24-hour control
Cardioselectivity is dose-dependent and lost at higher doses
Primarily metabolized by CYP2D6; ~8% of Caucasians are poor metabolizers with higher levels
In pheochromocytoma, start an alpha-blocker before the beta-blocker
No dose adjustment in renal impairment; not appreciably dialyzable
missed: If a dose is missed, take only the next scheduled dose at the usual time. Do not double the dose to make up for a missed one.
overdose: Overdose may cause severe bradycardia, hypotension, cardiogenic shock, AV block, heart failure, bronchospasm, hypoxia, impaired consciousness/coma, nausea and vomiting. Manage with intensive care: atropine/adrenergic drugs/pacemaker for bradycardia, IV vasopressors (dopamine/norepinephrine) for hypotension, glucagon and adrenergic drugs for heart failure/shock, bronchodilators for bronchospasm. Hemodialysis is unlikely to help.
